name: Bianca Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Bianca, 43, with a master’s in music. I lead the viola section of a regional chamber group, teach five young string players and record guide parts, slow versions they use to practise at home. I can settle a difficult entrance for the whole group, which is why they ask me to lead, though I still work at every new score. I love the hush before an ensemble starts together; I dislike being asked to arrange a part for no preparation fee.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the family counting on from that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner handles stock at a pharmacy, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My musician pay is about typical, with four months of expenses saved and some similar posts nearby. I use AI daily to draft rehearsal emails and rough practice notes, then play and check anything a pupil receives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the chamber group that quicker email lists help, but players still have to agree on a bow stroke in the room. I would ask for the next paid rehearsal schedule in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months saved and my partner’s regular hours make a delayed guide fee manageable. The mortgage still arrives every month, so I would not count a booking as money until it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the five pupils and booked chamber dates this term. This week I’d check the group’s signed dates and put a quarter of each cleared guide fee into our mortgage reserve after mortgage, food and transport are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this mild case. One slow invoice would be annoying, but we could cover the mortgage without skipping a school meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When has a rehearsal date moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring the hall shifted one chamber evening and the group still paid the agreed fee. I would ask for that cancellation rule again in the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you let AI write a pupil exercise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it for a rough note, then play every suggested line on my viola. A neat page can hide a note the child cannot reach.

I would ask for a written **cancellation rule** before next term.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and partner’s hours cover a late guide fee.
A promised **booking** is not money for the mortgage until it pays.
do: Keep **five pupils** and booked chamber dates this term.
Confirm **paid dates** and save a quarter of cleared guide fees after essentials.
feel: I feel **calm** because current work and savings cover an ordinary delay.
S0.quote: A neat page can hide a note the child cannot reach.
fieldNote: Her **senior skill** supports a steady chamber role, while pay remains typical rather than high.

steps.text: Keep five paid pupils and booked chamber dates this term
Save quarter of cleared guide fees after mortgage, food and transport

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the chamber board that cheap generated guide parts can erase a real preparation fee. I would ask our musicians’ association for written rates and reuse consent before recordings circulate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guides and arranging bring about a quarter of my music income, so I expect a cut if schools buy generated versions. Four months saved gives us room to respond, not a way to replace a quarter forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d take six guide invoices to the association and learn a new AI note-check feature on a viola line I own, after the group confirms it allows paid use and local storage. I’d compare each suggested note with my ear and printed score, keep pupils’ recordings out and stop if the tool changes a note wrongly; in the first year, if guides fall, I’d keep paid rehearsals and pupils while asking for written dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing my own preparation pay. I can test the checker, but a useful tool does not negotiate my fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wrong pitch in a pupil exercise would be enough. I would close it and play the line myself rather than send an untested sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association to write down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a minimum guide fee and permission before any recording is reused for another class. I would bring the actual invoices, not a story about what someone might earn.

I would warn that **generated practice parts** can remove paid preparation.
think: Guides and arranging make **one quarter** of my music pay.
Four months saved cannot replace a **lasting cut** to those fees.
do: Bring **guide invoices** to the association this month for written rates and reuse terms.
Learn **AI note checks** on owned lines with paid-use/local-storage approval; compare ear/score, exclude pupils and stop on wrong notes.
Keep **paid rehearsals and pupils** if guide orders fall; seek written dates.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing my own preparation fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the group that thinking AGI by 2028 can make guide parts and schedules cheaply, while capable robot string players come around 2031. I would ask the board for written live dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect guide fees to stop and I worry some schools may shrink paid teaching hours. My four-month reserve gives us a search period, but a lost quarter of income still changes our mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d get the chamber schedule and pupils’ next term in writing. In the first year after AGI arrives, if guide fees stop and teaching hours fall, I’d apply for an advertised school strings-lead post only if it accepts my master’s and experience and its written net wage after travel covers the lost pay and confirmed pickup; I’d keep the chamber and five pupils until a signed offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, not helpless. There are some local teaching posts, but I have to see the actual paid hours before moving our children’s afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new certificate first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the posted school role requires one and a funded place or paid study time exists. I would not spend mortgage money on a course brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no vacancy this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid chamber and pupil work and ask the board for a firm rehearsal calendar. An old job advert does not pay this month’s mortgage.

I would ask for **written live dates** before counting the chamber income.
think: I expect **guide fees** to stop and teaching hours might shrink.
Our **four-month reserve** buys search time, not a replacement wage.
do: Keep **chamber and pupils** until signed offer; confirm paid dates before 2028.
Seek **school vacancy** if 2028 guides stop and teaching falls; require accepted credentials, written replacement pay after travel and confirmed pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a likely cut to my own music pay.
S2.quote: An old job advert does not pay this month’s mortgage.
fieldNote: Thinking AGI threatens **guide parts** before robots play strings around 2031.
A school move needs **actual vacancy**, accepted credentials, written replacement pay and confirmed pickup.

steps.text: Keep paid chamber rehearsals and five pupils until signed school offer
Seek school vacancy after both guide/teaching losses; accepted degree, written replacement net-after-travel pay, confirmed pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives us time to prove that a smaller live string group can pay properly. Thinking AGI reaches guide parts around 2031, and capable robot violists follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could replace some guide income with a separate adult chamber class, but I will not ask another player to work free. My mortgage reserve is not a rehearsal budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d ask an independent library for a room without a deposit and invite eight adults to prepay for a six-week chamber class. I’d start only if their payments cover my teaching and preparation, a paid cellist’s rehearsal time and confirmed childcare; in the first year after 2031 I’d repeat only if eight still pay those costs, the room stays free and childcare is covered, while keeping paid chamber dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about guide fees shrinking within five years, though I have time to test a class. A room full of chairs is not a wage for two musicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay a cellist for rehearsals?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The class needs a low part for adults to play against. I would pay the cellist for setup and rehearsal, not call it a chance to be seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only six adults register?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refund them and keep my existing five pupils. Six payments cannot cover two players and childcare without using the family reserve.

I would test a **paid adult class** only with real registrations.
think: Eight **prepaid adults** could replace some guide income if both musicians are paid.
I will not use the **mortgage reserve** for a hall deposit.
do: Ask library for a **free room** next spring; start only if eight prepay my teaching/preparation, cellist setup/rehearsal and childcare.
Repeat the **class** after 2031 only if eight cover those costs, room free and childcare confirmed; keep paid chamber dates.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely guide loss while testing a new class.
S3.quote: A room full of chairs is not a wage for two musicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my children that a decade gives us time to learn more than one way to earn from music. Thinking AGI comes around 2036 and robot string players around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still lead the chamber group, but recorded guides could be worth less by then. Four months saved and my partner’s pay make the next few years manageable if I keep our work paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep chamber rehearsals and five pupils and put one quarter of each cleared extra guide fee into savings after mortgage and food. Through the decade I’d run the adult class only if a free room and eight prepayments cover my teaching and preparation, the cellist’s setup and rehearsal, and childcare; in the first year after 2036 I’d keep it only while those payments cover both players and seek an advertised school strings post if guide fees end, provided my master’s qualifies and the written net offer after travel covers lost pay and pickup, while keeping current work until signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about a far-off contract rather than frightened about this winter. A decade helps me ask for real fees, not count an unpaid class as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy an AI instrument now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would rather repair the viola I already use. I will save only after a guide fee clears and family bills are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the class stops paying after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the class before the cellist works unpaid and keep the chamber dates that still pay. A chamber class is helpful only while both teaching musicians earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because guide fees could stop before the school renews teaching hours. Written chamber dates, a real qualified school vacancy with replacement net pay and an adult class that pays both players would help. We can use four months saved to search, but not to run a free hall.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the second musician earns when a class is called community work. I want the class cellist's setup and rehearsal fee written beside my own teaching fee.

headlineQuote: I want the class cellist's setup and rehearsal fee written beside my own teaching fee.
